title: Fluid Intelligence Peak
shortDescription: Novel-problem reasoning with no reliance on prior knowledge — solving patterns you've genuinely never seen before.
longDescription: Fluid Intelligence Peak extends the Raven's Progressive Matrices paradigm toward its harder, more novel end — the family of "distribution of three" rules, where a Latin-square arrangement means every row and every column contains the same three values, just never in the same order. Recognizing this rule requires checking a grid two ways at once (across the row AND down the column), which is genuinely harder to spot than a simple row/column constant, and closer to what fluid intelligence research means by reasoning that doesn't reduce to a memorized rule.
sourceNote: Same real-SVG generation and programmatic verification approach as Abstract Reasoning Pro (see that file's sourceNote) — every grid is genuinely rendered, every correct answer is derived from the rule in code and checked to be the sole matching option before inclusion. The distribution-of-three (Latin square) rule family is weighted more heavily here than in Abstract Reasoning Pro specifically because it's a structurally different, less immediately obvious rule than 'this attribute is constant along a row/column' — closer to genuinely novel-pattern reasoning than a straightforward progression.

sections.name: Novel Matrices
sections.description: 3x3 grids, weighted toward distribution-of-three (Latin square) rules where every row and column contains the same three values.
sections.instructions: Check both across each row and down each column before answering — some of these grids aren't solvable by looking at just one direction.

scoringDimensions.label: Fluid Intelligence
scoringDimensions.description: Novel non-verbal reasoning, weighted toward distribution-of-three and multi-attribute rule types.

resultRanges.title: Developing
resultRanges.description: The distribution-of-three grids in particular are difficult to crack right now — recognizing a Latin-square pattern takes a different kind of scan than a simple row/column check.
recommendations: For each grid, explicitly list what's present in the row so far, then what's present in the column so far — the missing cell is often forced by both at once
Return to Abstract Reasoning Pro to build up simpler rule-recognition first
Don't assume the rule is a simple repeat — check whether all three values just appear in different order instead

resultRanges.title: Average
resultRanges.description: Simpler novel rules land, but the denser distribution-of-three and triple-attribute grids are still frequently missed.
recommendations: Practice specifically on Latin-square grids until the 'check row AND column' habit becomes automatic
Slow down on grids where no attribute looks constant anywhere — that's usually the signal it's a distribution rule

resultRanges.title: Strong
resultRanges.description: Reliably solves most novel rule types, including most distribution-of-three grids.
recommendations: Push into the triple-attribute items (shape by diagonal, color by row, rotation by column) specifically
This level of fluid reasoning is largely independent of vocabulary or specific knowledge — a genuine general-reasoning signal

resultRanges.title: Very Strong
resultRanges.description: Consistently solves even the densest, most novel grid types quickly.
recommendations: This is a strong, genuine fluid-intelligence signal — notice where novel-problem-solving shows up as an advantage in unfamiliar work
Compare this result with Abstract Reasoning Pro's — a gap between them is informative about which rule types you find easiest

resultRanges.title: Exceptional
resultRanges.description: Near-perfect performance even on the hardest, most novel distribution and multi-attribute rule types.
recommendations: This is an elite fluid-intelligence result — reasoning through genuinely unfamiliar structure quickly and accurately
Consider how this strength applies to real novel-problem domains you haven't encountered before
